(CNN) -- Farrah Fawcett, the actress known worldwide for her beauty and her role on "Charlie's Angels," is reportedly seriously ill and may be close to death after a long battle with cancer. Farrah Fawcett, seen here in 2004, is featured in a documentary about her fight with cancer. A documentary, which airs Friday night on NBC, will feature an intimate look at her life since being diagnosed with the disease. On Thursday, Larry King talked with Candy Spelling, a close friend of Fawcett. Her husband, the late Aaron Spelling, produced "Charlie's Angels." Spelling talks about her relationship with Fawcett and why she believes she did the documentary. The following is an edited version of the interview. Larry King: Did you first meet Farrah in connection with getting that part? Candy Spelling: Yes. Actually, she did a lot of small, little parts in the movies for Aaron starting around 1973. So it's been, my God, 36, 37 years since I, you know, first met her.  Watch Candy Spelling talk about her friendship with Farrah Fawcett » . King: So you knew her well during all that time? Spelling: Yes. King: Did you know about her getting picked to be on "Charlie's Angels?" Spelling: I remember. She did some small roles. I think the one that Aaron really decided he was really going to use her was this American beauty pageant and, also, it was like "Murder on Flight 502." He did the 90-minute versions. King: Movie of the week? Spelling: Right. Movie of the weeks. King: When did you know she had cancer? Spelling: I found out about a year -- when I first heard, I don't know if it was a year or two years ago when we first heard, and I contacted her. I hadn't talked to her in a while. She said, "I'm going to be all right, Candy. Everything is going to be all right." King: Why do you think, Candy, she did the documentary? Spelling: I think that she wanted to give other people courage that, you know, are fighting this kind of thing. I know how, you know, devastating the press, you know, was with Aaron when he had cancer. And it's just so difficult. And I mean, you know, it's hard to have a private life at that point. King: Why do the tabloids get so tough on someone in such pain? Spelling: It's news. It's kind of a sad thing. I'm always so sorry to see it. But, you know, people believe what they see, and a lot of times, we don't know how true it really is.

(CNN) — Farrah Fawcett, the actress known worldwide for her beauty and her role on “Charlie’s Angels,” is reportedly seriously ill and may be nearing death after a long battle with cancer.

Fawcett, pictured here in 2004, is the subject of a documentary about her fight against the disease. Airing Friday night on NBC, the documentary offers an intimate look at her life since her diagnosis.

On Thursday, Larry King spoke with Candy Spelling, a close friend of Fawcett. Spelling’s late husband, Aaron Spelling, produced “Charlie’s Angels.” She discussed her relationship with Fawcett and why she believes the actress chose to make the documentary.

The following is an edited version of the interview.

**Larry King:** Did you first meet Farrah in connection with her getting that part?

**Candy Spelling:** Yes. Actually, she appeared in a number of small movie roles for Aaron beginning around 1973. So it has been, my God, 36 or 37 years since I first met her.

*Watch Candy Spelling discuss her friendship with Farrah Fawcett »*

**King:** So you knew her well throughout that time?

**Spelling:** Yes.

**King:** Did you know about her being chosen for “Charlie’s Angels”?

**Spelling:** I remember. She had done some small roles. I think Aaron really decided he was going to use her after an American beauty pageant and also something like “Murder on Flight 502.” He made the 90-minute versions.

**King:** Movies of the week?

**Spelling:** Right. Movies of the week.

**King:** When did you learn that she had cancer?

**Spelling:** I found out about a year—I do not know whether it was one or two years ago when we first heard—and I contacted her. I had not spoken with her in a while. She said, “I’m going to be all right, Candy. Everything is going to be all right.”

**King:** Why do you think, Candy, that she made the documentary?

**Spelling:** I think she wanted to give courage to other people who are fighting this kind of illness. I know how devastating the press coverage was when Aaron had cancer. It is just so difficult. At that point, it is hard to have a private life.

**King:** Why are the tabloids so harsh toward someone in such pain?

**Spelling:** It is news. It is rather sad, and I am always so sorry to see it. But people believe what they see, and often we do not know how much of it is actually true.

(CNN) — Farrah Fawcett, internationally recognized for her looks and for starring in “Charlie’s Angels,” is said to be gravely ill and possibly nearing death following a lengthy struggle with cancer.

Fawcett, pictured in 2004, is the subject of an NBC documentary scheduled to air Friday night. The program offers a personal view of her life after her cancer diagnosis.

On Thursday, Larry King interviewed Fawcett’s longtime friend Candy Spelling, whose late husband, Aaron Spelling, produced “Charlie’s Angels.” Spelling discussed how she knew Fawcett and explained why she thought the actress chose to make the documentary. Below is an edited transcript of their conversation.

**Larry King:** Did you originally meet Farrah when she was being considered for that role?

**Candy Spelling:** Yes. Beginning around 1973, Aaron cast her in a number of minor movie roles. So, my goodness, it has been about 36 or 37 years since I first met her.

*Watch Candy Spelling discuss her friendship with Farrah Fawcett »*

**King:** Were the two of you close throughout those years?

**Spelling:** Yes.

**King:** Were you aware when she was selected for “Charlie’s Angels”?

**Spelling:** I remember it. She had appeared in several smaller parts. I believe Aaron truly decided he wanted to continue using her after an American beauty pageant project and something like “Murder on Flight 502.” He made the 90-minute formats.

**King:** Movies of the week?

**Spelling:** Yes, movies of the week.

**King:** When did you learn that she had cancer?

**Spelling:** I heard the news perhaps a year ago—or possibly two years ago; I’m not certain exactly when we first found out. I reached out to her because we had not spoken for some time. She told me, “I’m going to be all right, Candy. Everything is going to be all right.”

**King:** Candy, what do you think motivated her to make the documentary?

**Spelling:** I believe she hoped to encourage other people facing the same kind of illness. I know how devastating the media attention was when Aaron had cancer. It is extremely difficult, and maintaining any privacy at that stage is hard.

**King:** Why are tabloids so harsh toward people who are already suffering?

**Spelling:** Because it is considered news, which is unfortunate. It always saddens me to see that happen. People tend to accept what they read or see, even though we often cannot be sure how much of it is actually true.

### ENTERTAINMENT REPORT: FARRAH FAWCETT SERIOUSLY ILL

**ANCHOR:**  
Tonight, concern is growing for actress Farrah Fawcett, the 1970s television icon whose battle with cancer has taken a serious turn.

Fawcett, 62, became an international star as one of the original cast members of *Charlie’s Angels*. Her famous red swimsuit poster became one of the defining images of the decade, but she later pursued more demanding dramatic roles, earning critical praise for television films including *The Burning Bed*.

The actress was diagnosed with anal cancer in 2006. After treatment, doctors initially declared her cancer-free, but the disease later returned and spread to her liver. In recent weeks, she has reportedly been hospitalized as family and longtime companion Ryan O’Neal remain close by.

Her struggle is being documented in the NBC special *Farrah’s Story*, which follows Fawcett through treatment in the United States and Germany. Friends say she wanted viewers to see not only the physical toll of cancer but also her determination to fight it.

Her physician has described her condition as serious. Representatives for the actress are asking the public to respect her privacy while continuing to keep her in their thoughts.

---

### LARRY KING Q&A: CANDY SPELLING

**LARRY KING:** Candy, when you hear that Farrah Fawcett is seriously ill, what goes through your mind?

**CANDY SPELLING:** First, sadness. Farrah represents such a vivid time in Hollywood. She seemed full of energy and optimism. Whatever public image people remember, there is a real woman and a family enduring something terribly difficult.

**KING:** Did you know her well?

**SPELLING:** We crossed paths socially, but I would not describe us as intimate friends. Hollywood can make everyone appear closer than they really are. Still, illness touches people beyond friendship. You feel compassion for her and for everyone around her.

**KING:** Your late husband, Aaron Spelling, helped define television during the era when Farrah became a star. What made her so important?

**SPELLING:** She had something the camera immediately understood. She was glamorous, certainly, but there was also warmth and accessibility. Millions of young women wanted her hair and copied her style. That kind of connection cannot be manufactured.

**KING:** Was it difficult for actresses then to move beyond being viewed as a television beauty?

**SPELLING:** Very difficult. Once the public decides who you are, changing that perception takes courage. Farrah took serious dramatic roles and showed that she wanted to be judged as an actress, not simply as an image on a poster.

**KING:** She has allowed cameras to follow her cancer treatment. Is that a brave decision?

**SPELLING:** I think it can be, provided it is truly her decision. Cancer is frightening and often private. By showing the reality of treatment, she may help people feel less alone and encourage them to speak with their doctors.

**KING:** Some critics say such a program is too personal.

**SPELLING:** That is understandable, but Farrah has lived much of her life in public. If she believes telling this story gives meaning to what she is experiencing, then that choice deserves respect.

**KING:** What would you say to her tonight?

**SPELLING:** I would say that people remember more than the photograph and more than *Charlie’s Angels*. They remember her strength, her performances and the joy she brought them. I would tell her that many people are praying for her.

**KING:** Candy Spelling, thank you for joining us.

**SPELLING:** Thank you, Larry.
